questions.question: What is 'present bias'?

options.A: people overvalue immediate rewards over long-term payoffs

questions.correct_answer_text: people overvalue immediate rewards over long-term payoffs

steps: 'People have a tendency to overvalue immediate rewards over long-term payoffs.'

questions.question: In the famous money study, what did most people choose?

options.A: less money now, even though they'd end up less well-off

questions.correct_answer_text: less money now, even though they'd end up less well-off

steps: Most people chose less money now over more money later.

questions.question: Why do people procrastinate, according to the article?

options.A: because of present bias

questions.correct_answer_text: because of present bias

steps: Present bias is also the reason why people procrastinate.

questions.question: Why should you never go food shopping when hungry?

options.A: you overvalue the immediate reward of food

steps: When hungry, immediate rewards (food) seem more valuable, so you overbuy.

questions.question: What is one way to overcome the tendency to spend money immediately?

questions.question: What is the 'sunk-cost fallacy'?

options.A: the idea that because you've invested, you should persist no matter what
options.B: the idea that invested money is lost

questions.correct_answer_text: the idea that because you've invested, you should persist no matter what

steps: The sunk-cost fallacy: because you've invested time or money, you should persist.

questions.explanation: It often works against our best interests.

questions.question: What is a 'fallacy'?

options.A: an idea often believed to be true but which is false

questions.correct_answer_text: an idea often believed to be true but which is false

steps: 'A fallacy is an idea that is often believed to be true, but which is, in fact, false.'

questions.explanation: The sunk-cost idea is a fallacy.

questions.question: In the chocolate cake study, what made people more likely to eat the cake?

options.A: being told the cake required a significant investment of time and money

questions.correct_answer_text: being told the cake required a significant investment of time and money

steps: Those told the cake was expensive and far away were more likely to eat it all.

questions.question: Even though they felt full, why did people eat the cake?

options.A: because of the sunk-cost fallacy

questions.question: Which is an example of the sunk-cost fallacy in daily life?

questions.question: What does 'falling prey to' in the article mean?

questions.question: What is the 'law of diminishing returns'?

options.A: after a point, investing more does not lead to increased benefits

questions.correct_answer_text: after a point, investing more does not lead to increased benefits

steps: After a certain point, more money or effort does not bring more benefit.
solution.summary: Diminishing returns = less benefit per effort.

questions.explanation: More input gives less extra output.

questions.question: What example shows the law of diminishing returns?

options.A: inviting 20 or 30 people to paint one room

questions.correct_answer_text: inviting 20 or 30 people to paint one room

steps: Too many helpers make the decorating inefficient.

questions.explanation: At first more help is constructive.

questions.question: What does the pizza example teach us?

options.A: the first few slices are great, but then it becomes less pleasant
options.C: you should eat all the pizza

questions.correct_answer_text: the first few slices are great, but then it becomes less pleasant

steps: The first slices are great, but the benefit drops as you eat more.

questions.explanation: It shows diminishing returns.

questions.question: What lesson does the article draw from the law of diminishing returns?

options.A: doing your best is good enough - don't overdo things

questions.correct_answer_text: doing your best is good enough - don't overdo things

steps: 'It is really a reminder that doing your best is good enough.'
